title: Docker Storage — Volumes, Bind Mounts, overlayfs
subtitle: How container filesystems are assembled and where data survives container deletion

nodes.label:
Writable Layer
Container diff (ephemeral)
Deleted on docker rm

Image Layers (read-only)
FROM ubuntu → RUN apt → COPY

Bind Mount
Host path → container path

panels.title: Volume commands
panels.body:
Named volume (managed by Docker):
  docker volume create pgdata
  docker run -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres
  docker volume ls
  docker volume inspect pgdata
  docker volume rm pgdata     # fails if container still using it
  docker volume prune         # remove all unused volumes

Bind mount (host directory):
  docker run -v /host/src:/app/src node   # absolute path
  docker run -v $(pwd):/app node          # current dir (dev workflow)

tmpfs (RAM, no disk write):
  docker run --tmpfs /tmp:size=100m nginx  # ephemeral, in-memory

panels.title: overlayfs — how image layers stack
panels.body:
Image layers (read-only, bottom to top):
  layer 0: ubuntu:22.04 base (120 MB)
  layer 1: RUN apt-get install nginx (40 MB)
  layer 2: COPY ./html /var/www/html (2 MB)

Container adds:
  layer 3: writable diff layer (starts empty)

overlayfs merges them into one unified view.
Read: searches top-down; returns first match.
Write: copy-on-write — file copied to writable layer before modification.

Each container gets its own writable layer → same image,
many containers, only one copy of read-only layers on disk.

panels.title: Named volume vs bind mount
pros: Named volume: Docker manages location, portable across hosts, easy backup/restore with docker run --volumes-from
Bind mount: real-time code sync for dev, easy to inspect files from host, no volume creation needed
cons: Named volume: opaque location (/var/lib/docker/volumes/), harder to directly edit files from host
Bind mount: ties container to host filesystem layout, permission mismatches (host UID ≠ container UID) common
